entries.topicDescription: Core Android building blocks: intents, broadcast receivers, the manifest, and services.

tips.title: Explicit intents target a specific component; implicit intents ask the system to find one
tips.content:
An explicit intent names the exact component (by class) that should
handle it — used for navigating within your own app, where you know
precisely which Activity or Service should respond.

An implicit intent describes an action (VIEW, SEND, DIAL) and lets the
system match it against every installed app's declared intent filters,
letting the user pick from whichever apps can handle it — used for
inter-app actions like sharing content or opening a URL.

tips.title: Intent extras must be Parcelable or Serializable, and Parcelable is strongly preferred
tips.content:
Only primitive types and objects implementing Parcelable or Serializable
can be passed as Intent extras — Serializable relies on reflection and is
significantly slower, with more allocation overhead, than Parcelable's
explicit read/write implementation.

Data classes can implement Parcelable with minimal boilerplate using the
@Parcelize annotation, which generates the implementation at compile
time — pass only small amounts of data through Intent extras, since the
system enforces a strict total size limit (roughly 1MB) across the whole
Bundle.
tips.codeSnippet:
@Parcelize
data class UserSummary(val id: String, val name: String) : Parcelable

intent.putExtra("user", UserSummary("u1", "Ahmed"))
val user = intent.getParcelableExtra<UserSummary>("user") // fast, no reflection

tips.title: PendingIntents must declare mutability explicitly on Android 12+
tips.content:
A PendingIntent lets another component (the system, a notification, a
widget) execute your Intent later, on your app's behalf and with your
app's permissions — a mutable PendingIntent given to an untrusted party
can theoretically have its underlying Intent modified before execution,
which is a security risk.

Android 12 (API 31) requires every PendingIntent to explicitly specify
FLAG_MUTABLE or FLAG_IMMUTABLE — omitting both now throws an exception at
runtime, whereas older versions defaulted silently to mutable.
tips.codeSnippet:
val pendingIntent = PendingIntent.getActivity(
    context, requestCode, intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE // required explicitly since API 31
)

tips.title: Intent filters in the manifest declare what implicit intents a component can handle
tips.content:
A component only receives implicit intents matching an <intent-filter>
declared for it in the manifest — the filter specifies which actions,
categories, and data types/schemes it accepts, and Android matches
incoming implicit intents against every declared filter across all
installed apps.

A component can declare multiple intent filters to handle several
distinct implicit-intent scenarios, but each filter must independently
match action, category, AND data for the intent to be routed to that
component.
tips.codeSnippet:
<activity android:name=".ShareActivity">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
        <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

tips.title: App Links with autoVerify make your app the default handler for a domain's URLs
tips.content:
A plain deep-link intent filter still shows a disambiguation dialog
('Open with: Browser / Your App') every time, since the system can't
verify you actually own the domain being linked to.

android:autoVerify="true" combined with a Digital Asset Links JSON file
hosted at the domain's /.well-known/assetlinks.json path proves domain
ownership, letting the system open matching links directly in your app
without the chooser dialog.
tips.codeSnippet:
<intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
    <data android:scheme="https" android:host="example.com" />
</intent-filter>

tips.title: FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK and related flags control how an Intent affects the back stack
tips.content:
Intent flags change task-stack behavior beyond what launchMode alone
controls — FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK starts the Activity in a new task (or
an existing one if it's already running), FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP clears
any Activities above a matching existing instance instead of stacking a
new one on top.

Starting an Activity from a non-Activity context (a Service, a
BroadcastReceiver, an Application-level singleton) requires
FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK explicitly, since there's no existing task context
to launch into otherwise.

tips.title: Manifest-registered receivers persist app-wide; context-registered ones follow their owner's lifecycle
tips.content:
A <receiver> declared in the manifest is registered system-wide as soon
as the app is installed and stays active even when your app isn't
running — the system can wake your app via a broadcast, which is powerful
but also why it's now restricted for many implicit system broadcasts.

A dynamically registered receiver (context.registerReceiver()) only
receives broadcasts while the registering component is alive, and must
be explicitly unregistered (typically in onStop/onDestroy) to avoid a
leaked receiver reference.

tips.title: Android 8+ restricts most implicit broadcasts from waking apps via the manifest
tips.content:
Prior to Android 8 (API 26), a manifest-declared receiver could listen for
almost any system broadcast (connectivity changes, for example) and be
woken up even when the app wasn't running — this was a major source of
battery drain across the ecosystem from many apps all waking
simultaneously.

Most implicit system broadcasts now only reach dynamically registered
receivers (registered while the app is actually running); a small set of
explicitly exempted broadcasts (like BOOT_COMPLETED) still work via the
manifest.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- No longer reliably delivered via manifest registration on API 26+ -->
<receiver android:name=".ConnectivityReceiver">
    <intent-filter><action android:name="android.net.conn.CONNECTIVITY_CHANGE" /></intent-filter>
</receiver>
<!-- register this dynamically at runtime instead -->

tips.title: LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated — prefer in-process alternatives
tips.content:
LocalBroadcastManager was designed for broadcasting events entirely
within your own app's process, avoiding the security and performance
overhead of a system-wide broadcast — but it's now deprecated in favor of
modern reactive alternatives that fit better with coroutines and Compose.

A SharedFlow, an event bus built on Flow, or simple direct callback
interfaces between components generally replace LocalBroadcastManager
cleanly, with better lifecycle-awareness and less indirection than
broadcast-based event delivery.

tips.title: Ordered broadcasts let receivers run in priority order and optionally abort propagation
tips.content:
A normal broadcast delivers to all matching receivers roughly
simultaneously, in no guaranteed order, and none can affect delivery to
others. An ordered broadcast (sendOrderedBroadcast) delivers to receivers
sequentially based on their declared android:priority, and any receiver
can call abortBroadcast() to stop it from propagating further down the
chain.

This is useful for scenarios like an SMS-receiving app needing first
refusal on incoming messages, but it's a less common pattern in modern
Android development given the broader shift away from broadcasts for
intra-app communication.
tips.codeSnippet:
<receiver android:name=".HighPriorityReceiver" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter android:priority="999">
        <action android:name="com.example.EVENT" />
    </intent-filter>
</receiver>
// this receiver's onReceive() can call abortBroadcast() to block lower-priority receivers

tips.title: android:exported must now be declared explicitly for components with intent filters
tips.content:
Prior to Android 12 (API 31), a component with an intent filter but no
explicit android:exported attribute defaulted to exported="true",
silently exposing it to other apps — a common, easy-to-miss security
issue.

Android 12 requires android:exported to be declared explicitly for any
component with an intent filter; the app won't even install without it,
forcing a deliberate decision about whether the component should be
reachable from outside your app.
tips.codeSnippet:
<receiver
    android:name=".MyReceiver"
    android:exported="false"> <!-- required explicitly on API 31+ -->
    <intent-filter><action android:name="com.example.INTERNAL_EVENT" /></intent-filter>
</receiver>

tips.title: RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED restricts a dynamically registered receiver to your own app
tips.content:
The android:exported manifest attribute only applies to statically
declared receivers — a dynamically registered receiver (via
context.registerReceiver()) had no equivalent way to restrict its
visibility to only your own app's broadcasts until Android 13 (API 33).

RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED explicitly marks a dynamic receiver as internal-
only, and RECEIVER_EXPORTED marks it as intentionally open to other apps
— on API 33+, one of the two flags is now required when registering a
receiver for a non-system broadcast action.
tips.codeSnippet:
ContextCompat.registerReceiver(
    context, myReceiver, IntentFilter("com.example.INTERNAL_EVENT"),
    ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED // explicit intra-app-only scope
)

tips.title: Manifest merging combines declarations from every module and library dependency
tips.content:
In a multi-module or library-dependent app, the final AndroidManifest.xml
installed on the device is produced by merging the app module's manifest
with every dependency's own manifest — permissions, components, and
meta-data all get combined, which can introduce unexpected entries you
never declared directly.

Running ./gradlew app:processDebugManifest (or checking the merged
manifest report in Android Studio's build output) reveals exactly what
ended up in the final manifest, which is invaluable for tracking down an
unexpected permission or component pulled in transitively by a library.

tips.title: Dangerous permissions need both a manifest declaration and a runtime request
tips.content:
Declaring a permission in the manifest via <uses-permission> is necessary
but not sufficient for 'dangerous'-protection-level permissions (camera,
location, contacts) — on API 23+, the app must also explicitly request
the permission at runtime and handle the user's grant/deny response,
since the manifest declaration alone no longer auto-grants it at install
time.

'Normal'-protection-level permissions (internet access, vibration) are
granted automatically at install time from the manifest declaration
alone, with no runtime prompt needed — the distinction matters for
planning which permissions need in-app request flows at all.
tips.codeSnippet:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.CAMERA" /> <!-- necessary but not sufficient -->

// still required at runtime:
requestPermissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)

tips.title: android:process lets a component run in a separate process from the rest of the app
tips.content:
By default, every component in an app runs in a single shared process —
but declaring android:process=":remote" on a component (commonly a
Service) spins it up in a genuinely separate OS process, isolated from
the main app process's memory and, notably, from a crash in the main
process.

This adds real complexity: components across processes can't share memory
directly and must communicate via IPC (Binder, AIDL) instead of plain
method calls, so it's reserved for cases with a specific isolation need
(a crash-prone SDK, a memory-heavy background task) rather than a default
choice.
tips.codeSnippet:
<service
    android:name=".SyncService"
    android:process=":sync" /> <!-- runs in a separate process from the main app -->

tips.title: minSdkVersion, targetSdkVersion, and compileSdkVersion each control something different
tips.content:
minSdkVersion is the oldest Android version the app can even install on
— the compiler rejects APIs newer than this unless guarded. targetSdkVersion
tells the system which version's behavior your app was designed and
tested against, which changes runtime behavior (permission models,
background restrictions) even on newer devices, since the OS applies
compatibility behavior based on it.

compileSdkVersion is purely a build-time setting — which SDK's APIs and
lint rules are available while compiling — and has zero effect on runtime
behavior or which devices can install the app; it's normal, and
recommended, for compileSdkVersion to be higher than targetSdkVersion.

tips.title: The queries element declares which other apps' packages you're allowed to see
tips.content:
Android 11 (API 30) introduced package visibility filtering — by default,
queryIntentActivities() and similar package-querying APIs only return a
limited, curated set of results, hiding most other installed apps for
privacy reasons, unless you explicitly declare intent to interact with
them.

The <queries> manifest element declares which specific packages,
intent actions, or content provider authorities your app needs visibility
into — omitting a needed declaration causes package-query APIs to
silently return incomplete results instead of throwing an obvious error.
tips.codeSnippet:
<queries>
    <intent>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.SEND" />
        <data android:mimeType="text/plain" />
    </intent>
    <package android:name="com.whatsapp" />
</queries>

tips.title: Started services run independently of any caller; bound services are tied to their client's connection
tips.content:
A started service (via startService()/startForegroundService()) runs
independently once launched — it keeps running even if the component
that started it is destroyed, and must explicitly call stopSelf() or be
stopped externally.

A bound service (via bindService()) exists to provide a client-server
interface to other components while they're connected — it starts when
the first client binds and is destroyed once the last client unbinds, so
its lifetime is directly tied to active connections rather than an
independent running state.

tips.title: Foreground services require an ongoing notification and, since Android 14, a declared type
tips.content:
A foreground service must show a persistent notification within a few
seconds of starting, giving the user visible awareness that something is
running in the background consuming resources on their behalf — without
it, the system throws an exception and stops the service.

Android 14 (API 34) additionally requires declaring a specific foreground
service type (dataSync, mediaPlayback, location, etc.) both in the
manifest and when starting the service, and restricts which types are
allowed to be started depending on how the app was launched (from the
background vs. by direct user action).
tips.codeSnippet:
<service android:name=".SyncService" android:foregroundServiceType="dataSync" />

// starting it:
ServiceCompat.startForeground(this, notificationId, notification, ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_DATA_SYNC)

tips.title: IntentService is deprecated — use WorkManager or a CoroutineWorker instead
tips.content:
IntentService ran queued work items sequentially on a single background
thread and stopped itself once the queue was empty — but it's deprecated
since it doesn't cooperate with modern background execution limits and
has no built-in retry, constraint, or persistence support.

WorkManager (with a CoroutineWorker for coroutine-based implementations)
is the recommended replacement: it respects Doze/background restrictions
automatically, supports constraints (network availability, charging
state), and persists queued work across process death and even device
reboots.

tips.title: onStartCommand's return value controls what happens if the system kills and restarts the service
tips.content:
START_STICKY tells the system to recreate the service after it's killed
for memory, but delivers a null Intent to onStartCommand on restart —
appropriate for a service that doesn't rely on the original Intent's data
to resume its work (like a media player that can just resume its current
state).

START_REDELIVER_INTENT instead redelivers the last Intent that was
queued before the kill, appropriate for services that genuinely need that
data to resume correctly (an in-progress upload that needs the file URI
again); START_NOT_STICKY doesn't restart the service at all after a kill.

tips.title: Background execution limits since Android 8 restrict what a plain background Service can do
tips.content:
Since Android 8 (API 26), apps in the background are prevented from
freely starting background (non-foreground) services in most
circumstances — calling startService() from the background often throws
an IllegalStateException instead of silently starting the service the way
it did on older versions.

This pushed most genuine background-work use cases toward either
WorkManager (deferred, constraint-aware work) or a foreground service
with a visible notification (immediate, user-visible work) — a plain
background service started from the background is no longer a reliable
pattern on modern Android.

tips.title: ServiceConnection and AIDL enable structured communication with a bound service
tips.content:
Binding to a service gives you an IBinder, but working with it directly
as a raw IBinder is awkward — ServiceConnection's onServiceConnected
callback typically casts it to a custom Binder subclass (for same-process
binding) that exposes the service's actual public methods directly.

For cross-process binding (a different app, or a service in a separate
android:process), AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language) defines the
contract and generates the IPC marshalling code automatically, since a
plain custom Binder subclass only works safely within the same process.

tips.title: A Service runs on the main thread by default — it does not imply background execution
tips.content:
A common misconception is that simply being a Service means work runs off
the main thread automatically — a plain Service's callbacks
(onStartCommand, onBind) execute on the main thread just like an
Activity's, so blocking work inside them still freezes the UI exactly
like blocking work in an Activity would.

Genuine background execution requires explicitly moving work off the main
thread inside the service (a coroutine with Dispatchers.IO, a background
HandlerThread) — the 'background' in the term refers to the app's UI
visibility state, not automatically to which thread the code executes on.

tips.title: Services declared in a library manifest still require exported/permission review at merge time
tips.content:
A Service declared by a third-party SDK's own manifest merges into your
app's final manifest just like any of your own components — if that
service is exported and lacks a permission restriction, it becomes part
of your app's attack surface even though you never wrote or reviewed its
declaration directly.

Reviewing the merged manifest (not just your own module's source) is
especially important for services and receivers pulled in transitively,
since a poorly-secured component from a dependency is just as exploitable
as one you declared yourself.
tips.codeSnippet:
<!-- from a third-party library's manifest, merged into your final app -->
<service android:name="com.thirdparty.sdk.RemoteService" android:exported="true" />
<!-- review the merged manifest report to catch cases like this -->
